newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's native language gets its own TV channel.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's native language gets its own TV channel.

text.p: "Go mbeannai dia oraibh agus seo iad cinnlinte na nuachta."

The words mean "Good evening, here is the news". They will be among the first used on Thursday when Ireland's new television station is launched, broadcasting in an ancient tongue which most of the country does not use.
Teilifis na Gaeilge (Irish Television) is the country's first national Irish-language television channel.
It has been hailed as a major boost to the native tongue, a Celtic language spoken in Ireland for more than 2,500 years but now little used after centuries of decline and domination by English.
The channel will broadcast for three hours every day, featuring news, cartoons, music, documentaries, a soap opera and even Spanish soccer with commentary in Irish.

It opens with a drama in Irish written by and featuring Hollywood star Gabriel Byrne, followed by a special concert in Donegal. Irish President Mary Robinson and Prime Minister John Bruton will also appear on the opening night.

The launch of Teilifis na Gaeilge follows a long battle by activists to win the Irish language its own channel. Opponents argued that state money should not be spent on television programmes in a language spoken only by a tiny minority.
A recent survey estimated that only four percent of Ireland's 3.6 million people were completely fluent in Irish. A further nine percent could follow most conversations.
The channel cost the government 16 million punts ($26.13 million) to set up and will require a further 10 million punts in state funding each year.
But supporters of Irish say Teilifis na Gaeilge will ensure the language is saved from extinction and will boost a current revival of interest in Irish.

"This long-delayed newcomer to our airwaves will, hopefully, be seen as a watershed in our long -- but less than wholehearted -- struggle to make Irish a central part of what we are," the Irish Times said in an editorial.
"Without a television channel of its own, the Irish language is unlikely to survive in a world increasingly dominated by the media -- especially television."
Irish was marginalised and suppressed after England's colonisation of Ireland began in the 16th century.
It survives mainly in remote areas on the country's wild fringes, including the Connemara region where Teilifis na Gaeilge is based.
